suggestion.title: Child Process Spawning from VS Code Extension Runtime
suggestion.rationale: Malicious extensions often spawn shell processes (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash) to execute stealing payloads. Article does not specify technique, but common in extension-based attacks. Pipeline must detect this execution pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on code.exe or node.exe (extension host) spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash, or curl with suspicious arguments (curl to external IP, encoded commands). Extensions should use Node APIs; shell invocation is a major red flag. Baseline legitimate extensions and alert on anomalies.

suggestion.title: Typosquatted or Single-Letter-Variant Extension Names Installed
suggestion.rationale: Evil twin attacks rely on name similarity ('Prettier' → 'Prettier-Format'). Article title signals marketplace poisoning. Detection should look for installation of extensions whose names are within edit distance 2 of popular extensions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Maintain registry of top 100 popular VS Code extensions. When a new extension is installed via marketplace, compute Levenshtein distance to legitimate names. Flag installs with distance ≤2 and suspicious metadata (new publisher, zero reviews, unusual permissions). Cross-check against published CVEs and removal notices.

suggestion.title: Data Compression or Staging in VS Code Extension Directory Before Exfil
suggestion.rationale: Attackers typically stage exfiltrated data (credentials, SSH keys, source code) before transmission. Look for archive creation (zip, tar, 7z) or temporary file staging in ~/.vscode/extensions/ directory preceding outbound network activity.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for creation of .zip, .tar, .rar, .7z files in ~/.vscode or extension directories. Correlate with code.exe process spawning 7z, tar, or similar compression tools. Alert if compression is followed within minutes by DeviceNetworkEvents from code.exe or spawned processes to external IPs.

suggestion.title: Langflow RCE Exploitation via API Endpoint
suggestion.rationale: Article title explicitly flags 'Langflow RCE' as actively exploited, but pipeline extracted zero use cases. Langflow is a flow-based LLM orchestration framework; exploitation likely leverages unsafe deserialization or code-injection in pipeline nodes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect HTTP POST/PUT requests to Langflow API endpoints (/api/flows, /api/execute) originating from external IPs with JSON payloads containing shell metacharacters, Base64 blobs, or node-injection syntax. Correlate with unexpected child process spawning under Langflow service account.

suggestion.title: Apache Tomcat Post-Exploitation Process Spawning
suggestion.rationale: Article cites Tomcat vulnerability as actively exploited; typical Tomcat RCE leads to reverse shells or web shell deployment. Pipeline missed detecting child processes spawned under catalina.sh or java processes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for cmd.exe, powershell.exe, or /bin/bash child processes spawned with parent Tomcat/java process. Alert on base64-encoded commands, reverse-shell patterns (bash -i >& /dev/tcp/), or obfuscated variable expansion.

suggestion.title: N-central Privilege Escalation Post-Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article highlights N-central (SolarWinds product) flaw; N-central runs with SYSTEM privileges on Windows and often provides lateral movement pivot. Pipeline failed to suggest detection for privilege escalation via N-central exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect creation of high-privilege processes (SYSTEM/root) initiated from N-central agent service account. Flag unexpected network connections from N-central process to external C2 endpoints or lateral movement targets (NetBIOS, RDP, WinRM).

suggestion.title: RCE Reverse Shell Callback Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article describes active exploitation of remote-code-execution flaws. Pipeline omitted detection for post-exploitation callback behavior (C2 communication, exfiltration setup).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify outbound TCP connections from Langflow/Tomcat/N-central service processes to rare or suspicious external IPs/domains on high-numbered ports (4444, 5555, 8888, 9999). Correlate with PowerShell/cmd spawning and base64-encoded DNS queries.

suggestion.title: Vulnerable Application Version Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article does not provide specific CVE versions or patchable builds in the supplied text. Pipeline should have extracted product version footprints (User-Agent headers, banner grabs) from any embedded indicators.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Baseline Langflow, Tomcat, and N-central deployments by version signature. Detect connections to known-vulnerable versions via Server headers, default error pages, or endpoint response metadata. Flag any version < patched baseline.

suggestion.title: Web Shell Upload to Compromised Application Root
suggestion.rationale: Common post-RCE pattern: attackers upload web shells to application webroot for persistent access. Article's truncated state prevents extraction of specific file indicators, but pipeline should have inferred this pattern from 'actively exploited RCE' context.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor Tomcat webapps directory and Langflow static folders for unexpected .jsp, .aspx, .php, or .py file creation post-exploitation window. Alert on HTTP requests to newly-created files matching web shell signatures (eval, system, cmd patterns in response bodies).

suggestion.title: Suspicious npm Post-Install Script Execution
suggestion.rationale: Article states worm is 'hidden in... npm packages' and spreads by automatic republishing—indicating execution via install hooks. Pipeline missed detection of child processes spawned during package installation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unexpected child processes (powershell.exe, cmd.exe, curl, wget) spawned during npm install or yarn install execution. Correlate timing: process spawn within 5 seconds of package extraction. Flag if parent is npm/node and child is network-touching.

suggestion.title: Credential Exfiltration During Package Installation
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes 'credential-stealing worm.' Pipeline missed detection of environment variable and credential file access during npm operations.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Track access to .ssh, .aws, .git configs, NPMRC, and process environment during node execution. Flag reads of $HOME/.credentials, %APPDATA%\npm-cache, or environment variable dumps within install script context.

suggestion.title: npm Registry Republishing / Package Update Anomaly
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states malicious updates spread 'by republishing malicious updates.' Pipeline missed lateral movement phase—detecting unusual npm publish activity from compromised developer machines.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for 'npm publish' commands executed outside normal CI/CD windows or by non-service accounts. Correlate with previous credential access events. Flag republish of existing packages with version bumps or immediate re-release.

suggestion.title: Recursive npm Dependency Chain Traversal
suggestion.rationale: Article describes worm 'spread across software ecosystems'—indicating malware exploits transitive dependency resolution to reach downstream consumers. Pipeline did not model supply-chain propagation vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Track npm install operations and build the induced dependency graph. Identify packages with newly compromised transitive dependencies. Alert on first-time execution of install scripts for packages whose dependencies have been modified within 7 days.

suggestion.title: Outbound Network Connections from npm/Node Process
suggestion.rationale: Credential-stealing worm must exfiltrate credentials to attacker C2. Article implies data theft but pipeline extracted zero IOCs for C2 domains, suggesting missed exfiltration detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor outbound connections (HTTP/HTTPS) initiated by node.exe, npm.cmd, or yarn.cmd to non-standard ports or known non-library domains. Flag if connection occurs during install and resolves to recently registered domain or known malicious IP.

suggestion.title: Package Manifest Script Injection Detection
suggestion.rationale: npm packages execute preinstall/postinstall/prepare scripts defined in package.json. Article indicates worm uses this mechanism ('hidden in npm packages'), but pipeline did not generate detection for obfuscated or suspicious scripts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Extract and analyze package.json scripts from installed packages. Flag scripts that: (a) are base64/rot13 encoded, (b) fetch remote code, (c) exfiltrate environment variables, or (d) spawn processes with no relation to package purpose.

suggestion.title: Email Authentication Bypass via Whitelisted Domain with Failed DMARC/SPF
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers spoofed service@ringcentral[.]com with 'failed SPF and DMARC checks, and had no DKIM signature' but were still accepted 'because RingCentral was whitelisted.' This is a precise defense-evasion pattern exploiting organizational trust lists.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on emails from whitelisted domains/senders where authentication headers show failed SPF/DMARC/DKIM validation. Cross-reference with phishing-like subject lines (voicemail notifications, performance reviews, account verifications). Severity increases if sender domain is commonly spoofed service (RingCentral, Microsoft, Okta).

suggestion.title: MFA Token Capture via Adversary-in-the-Middle Phishing Flow
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'Microsoft adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) phishing flow that captured an MFA-approved authentication token.' Victims clicked embedded links to Greatness infrastructure and had tokens harvested post-MFA challenge.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect successful MFA sign-in events immediately followed (within 2–5 minutes) by anomalous Graph API calls or mailbox access from a VPS/VPN IP range. AiTM signatures: legitimate auth success → token stolen → token replayed from attacker infrastructure within same session window.

suggestion.title: Device-Code OAuth Phishing Flow
suggestion.rationale: Article names 'device-code phishing flow' as alternative vector to AiTM for harvesting credentials. Device-code flows are lower friction and increasingly abused by phishing kits targeting Microsoft 365.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect device-code authentication flows from high-risk ISPs (Shodan-indexed VPS/VPN ranges). Flag flows where user completes the code grant but the subsequent access token is not used from user's known locations. Cross-reference device-code grant URI with known phishing domains or typosquatting variants.

suggestion.title: Post-Compromise Microsoft Graph API Multi-Resource Enumeration
suggestion.rationale: Article states attackers 'enumerated Outlook mailboxes, Teams conversations, SharePoint sites, OneDrive files, contacts, calendars, and registered applications through Microsoft Graph, with access persisting for more than two weeks.' This is systematic discovery + collection post-compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect rapid bursts of Graph API calls spanning multiple resource types (/me/mailFolders, /me/drive, /me/joinedTeams, /me/ownedObjects, /me/calendar) from a single user/service principal within 30–60 minutes. Flag if baseline Graph usage is minimal but spike occurs post-authentication from VPN/VPS. Persistence >2 weeks indicates token replay cycle.

suggestion.title: Authentication Token Replay from VPS and Commercial VPN Infrastructure
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states attackers 'replayed Microsoft 365 authentication tokens from VPS and commercial VPN infrastructure.' This is post-compromise lateral movement and persistence using stolen tokens.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect successful authentications or service principal sign-ins where source IP is registered to known VPS/VPN providers (AWS, Azure, DigitalOcean, Linode, commercial VPN) AND geolocation is inconsistent with user baseline. Compare to legitimate sign-in windows; token replay typically occurs hours/days after initial compromise.

suggestion.title: Unauthorized OAuth Consent Grants and Service Principal Persistence Post-Compromise
suggestion.rationale: Article recommends auditing 'OAuth consent, Microsoft Graph activity' post-compromise, implying attackers grant malicious apps graph/mail permissions. This establishes persistence and enables ongoing enumeration and exfiltration.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect OAuth application consent grants approved during or shortly after suspicious sign-in events (VPS/VPN origin, failed auth chain). Flag new service principal or app registrations with Graph.Mail.Read or Mail.ReadWrite permissions. Cross-correlate with mailbox forwarding rules, delegate access, or app password creation.

suggestion.title: OAuth provider receives token-refresh storm from single Flowise instance
suggestion.rationale: Article states endpoint 'sends a refresh request to the configured OAuth provider'—no hunt for anomalous refresh patterns at the provider side. Attackers harvesting tokens will trigger burst of refresh RPC calls to Google/GitHub/etc.
log_sources: WAF logs for token-endpoint POST spikes

Correlate with upstream Flowise logs showing UC_10_4 activity. Provider logs will show refresh_token grant with client_id matching the stolen credentials.

suggestion.title: Downstream service authentication spike using stolen OAuth access tokens
suggestion.rationale: Article headline: vulnerability 'enables token theft for any connected service'—no detection for attacker leveraging stolen tokens against downstream services (Gmail, Slack, GitHub, etc.). Tokens are stolen to be used.
log_sources: OAuth scopes: Gmail audit, GitHub API logs, Slack workspace audit
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: After detecting successful token refresh (UC_10_4), hunt for unusual authentication to downstream services from the same Flowise instance or from external IPs using the stolen tokens. Look for API calls to services the Flowise deployment shouldn't normally access (e.g., if Flowise is a doc-processing app, unexpected Gmail/Slack API calls are anomalous).

suggestion.title: Same Flowise credentialId refreshed repeatedly in short window
suggestion.rationale: While UC_10_4 detects volume of refreshes, attackers will test token freshness/validity by re-refreshing the same credential multiple times. This is distinct from normal rotation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect same Web.url (specific credentialId) being hit with POST >=3 times within 60 seconds. Legitimate operations refresh each credential once per token-expiry cycle, not in rapid succession.

suggestion.title: Flowise stored credential material accessed outside normal operation
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies endpoint 'decrypts the stored credential (containing clientId, clientSecret, refresh_token)'—no detection for unauthorized access to credential storage. Attackers may also dump the encryption key or credential database.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor reads to Flowise credential storage directory (typically `.flowise/credentials` or similar) from processes other than the Flowise daemon, or detect SQL queries accessing the credentials table outside of the token-refresh API flow. Correlate with UC_10_2/10_3/10_4 activity from same source.

suggestion.title: Flowise instance makes unusual outbound OAuth token calls to new provider domains
suggestion.rationale: Article describes endpoint making refresh RPC to 'configured OAuth provider'—if attacker modifies stored credentials to point to attacker-controlled domain, outbound OAuth calls would leak tokens to external server.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect outbound HTTPS POST requests from Flowise instance to OAuth token endpoints (`oauth.googleapis.com`, `github.com/login/oauth/access_token`, etc.) where the destination domain is either new (not seen in baseline) or resolves to unexpected IPs. Attackers can redirect token-refresh calls to exfiltration servers.

suggestion.title: Flowise credentialId parameter fuzzing / sequential enumeration without 200 responses
suggestion.rationale: UC_10_3 detects successful enumeration via distinct URLs; should also detect FAILED enumeration attempts (404/401 responses to many sequential IDs), which is the recon phase before UC_10_2 exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect high volume of POST requests to `/api/v1/oauth2-credential/refresh/:credentialId` where the ID parameter is sequential (1,2,3... or UUID-like patterns) and status is NOT 200. Threshold: >=20 failed attempts in 10m from single source. This is reconnaissance before exploitation.

suggestion.title: N-able N-central Authentication Bypass Exploitation Attempts
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel allows for authentication bypass' — must detect HTTP requests to N-central authenticated endpoints without proper auth tokens, or using alternate authentication flows (cookie tampering, direct API access, header manipulation).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag HTTP 200 responses to N-central /api/ or /admin/ endpoints lacking authentication headers/cookies, or with malformed auth tokens. Cross-reference against login audit logs to detect resource access without corresponding authentication event in preceding 5-minute window.

suggestion.title: N-able N-central Asset Inventory and Patch Status Hunt
suggestion.rationale: CISA KEV with federal remediation due 2026-08-07 — article explicitly recommends 'quick check across fleet' for patch lag. Must enumerate N-central instances and validate patch status before deadline.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Service enumeration and port scanning for N-central default ports; extract version from banner or management console. Correlate against N-able security advisory for patched builds. Flag any instances running unpatched versions before 2026-08-07.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation Administrative Actions via Compromised N-central
suggestion.rationale: After successful auth bypass, attacker gains management console. Article implies console access — should detect configuration changes, user creation, policy pushes, or remote command execution without corresponding admin authentication audit trail.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect N-central configuration modifications, user account creation, policy changes, or remote execution events with no corresponding admin login event in preceding 10-minute window. Flag orphaned session tokens with escalated privileges.

suggestion.title: Lateral Movement via N-central Agent Deployment to Managed Endpoints
suggestion.rationale: N-central is enterprise management platform with broad endpoint visibility/control. Compromised N-central is pivot point — should detect unauthorized agent deployment, configuration push, or script execution to managed assets.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor N-central initiated endpoint deployments, agent updates, or configuration pushes without corresponding change management request. Correlate unusual deployment volume or targeting patterns with CVE-2026-18556 exploitation timeframe.

suggestion.title: Anomalous N-central API and Management Console Access Patterns
suggestion.rationale: Auth bypass suggests API or alternate channel exploitation. Should baseline normal access patterns (IPs, user agents, request types) and flag deviations consistent with automated or unauthorized exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish N-central API request baseline (legitimate admin IPs, user agents, endpoint paths). Flag bulk requests to /api/ endpoints from non-admin sources, high request volume within short window, requests with non-standard Content-Type or Accept headers, or path traversal attempts.

suggestion.title: N-central Authentication Bypass — Unauthenticated Access via Alternate Path
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'N-able N-central contains an authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel that allows for authentication bypass.' Pipeline produced zero use cases. This is the primary attack vector and should be hunted via HTTP access logs for 401→200 sequences or successful requests to non-standard auth endpoints.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Look for unauthenticated HTTP requests to N-central endpoints (port 443 typical) that receive 200 responses, or rapid 401→200 status transitions on alternate paths like /api/, /rpc/, or non-standard auth URIs. Spike in requests from external IPs post-2026-08-04 (KEV publication date) should trigger escalation.

suggestion.title: N-central Post-Compromise Lateral Movement Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'N-central contains an authentication bypass… allows for authentication bypass.' N-central is remote management software; once compromised via this CVE, the attacker gains control over managed systems. Pipeline failed to model post-compromise activity. Detect anomalous commands/connections issued through N-central to managed endpoints.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor N-central server for unusual outbound process execution or network connections to managed systems outside business hours or from non-baseline admin accounts. Flag execution of reconnaissance tools (whoami, ipconfig, dsquery) issued through N-central management protocols.

suggestion.title: N-central Management Server Enumeration & Asset Discovery
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies N-central as authentication-bypassed management platform. Post-compromise, attackers enumerate managed assets and relationships. Pipeline missed discovery phase entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect anomalous asset enumeration queries to N-central API or database (rapid queries to inventory endpoints) within minutes of initial breach. Monitor for DNS queries or network connections from N-central server to new/unexpected subnets after bypass is exploited.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-18556 Vulnerability Scanner Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'CISA KEV catalog only adds CVEs that have been observed exploited in the wild.' Standard asset-exposure hunt required; pipeline produced zero IOCs and zero hunts despite template guidance in article.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Match CVE-2026-18556 against all vulnerability scanner outputs, endpoint inventory, and network asset databases. Prioritize N-able N-central instances exposed to external networks or accessible via VPN. Track patch deployment status across fleet; patch-lag between CISA catalog publication (2026-08-04) and due date (2026-08-07) is high-risk window.

suggestion.title: N-central Remote Code Execution Post-Bypass
suggestion.rationale: Article does not explicitly mention RCE, but N-central is an RMM platform; authentication bypass directly enables execution of arbitrary commands on managed systems. Pipeline missed command-and-control and execution phases entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor N-central task/deployment logs for scheduled commands targeting unusual processes (cmd, powershell, rundll32) issued by system accounts or non-baseline admin IDs. Cross-correlate with EDR: flag processes spawned from N-central agent pid shortly after auth-bypass indicators.

suggestion.title: Federal Agency N-central Patch Compliance — Expedited Remediation Hunt
suggestion.rationale: Article: 'Federal patch due: 2026-08-07. Federal civilian agencies are required to remediate by the published due date.' Pipeline provided zero compliance hunt. Regulatory/audit risk is extreme; this should be a separate compliance-tracking detection.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: For federal civilian and DoD agencies: extract all N-central instances from inventory, cross-reference against patch compliance dashboards. Flag any N-central installations not patched by 2026-08-07 23:59 UTC for immediate escalation to compliance/legal. Daily audit snapshots from 2026-08-04 → 2026-08-08.

suggestion.title: Asset Exposure: N-able N-central Instances
suggestion.rationale: Article states CISA KEV is 'currently being exploited' and lists N-able N-central as target product. Pipeline output section explicitly references template `asset-exposure` but generated no UC to instantiate it.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Search for network listening ports and processes associated with N-able N-central (typically management port 8040 or variants). Correlate with vulnerability scanner output for CVE-2026-18556 exposure. High priority: CISA KEV due date is 2026-08-07.

suggestion.title: Authentication Bypass: Alternate-Path Access
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes 'authentication bypass using alternate path or channel.' This is the core attack step; no detection UC was generated despite being the vulnerability's defining behavior.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Hunt for authentication flows to N-able N-central that succeed without credential validation or via non-standard authentication channels (e.g., direct API calls, bypass of SSO, alternate API endpoints). Baseline normal authentication patterns first.

suggestion.title: Exploitation Attempts: CVE-2026-18556 Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article identifies CVE-2026-18556 as actively exploited. No scan-based or network-based detection UC was generated to identify exploitation requests (failed or successful).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for HTTP/HTTPS requests containing exploit patterns or CVE-2026-18556 indicators sent to N-able N-central services. Include failed attempts (403/401 followed by 200). Focus on external-facing instances.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation: Unauthorized Access After Auth Bypass
suggestion.rationale: After authentication bypass succeeds, attacker gains system access. Pipeline did not suggest UC for detecting post-compromise activity (credential access, data collection, lateral movement).
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate successful N-able N-central authentication (post-exploit window) with unusual process execution, file modifications in sensitive directories, or outbound network connections to attacker infrastructure.

suggestion.title: ClickFix Delivery Domain Access Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly references '250 ClickFix Domains' in the title as attack infrastructure; zero IOCs extracted. Detection must identify network traffic to known ClickFix distribution domains.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for network connections and DNS queries to known ClickFix distribution domains. Correlate browser process (Safari, Chrome) initiating connection with subsequent suspicious binary execution in ~/Downloads, /tmp, or cache paths. Domain-to-execution chaining improves fidelity.

suggestion.title: Browser Fingerprinting Script Execution Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article headline emphasizes 'browser fingerprinting to hide macOS malware lures'—fingerprinting is the core evasion mechanism. Detection should identify JavaScript conducting system capability probing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify browser processes executing JavaScript that enumerates system characteristics: Canvas/WebGL fingerprinting, user-agent parsing, timezone/locale/screen resolution queries, or CPU core enumeration. Obfuscated or high-entropy probe code signals evasion-aware malware.

suggestion.title: macOS Binary Execution Post-ClickFix Click
suggestion.rationale: Article describes ClickFix delivering malware specifically to macOS systems. Detection must correlate malicious domain click with payload execution.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: On macOS, correlate browser network connection to ClickFix domain with launch of suspicious downloaded binary (PKG, DMG, APP installers from ~/Downloads or /tmp). Alert on shell processes spawned by browser or xattr -d com.apple.quarantine execution.

suggestion.title: Suspicious macOS Download Execution Bypass
suggestion.rationale: ClickFix targeting macOS implies downloaded payloads bypass or abuse Gatekeeper/quarantine mechanisms to execute.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor ~/Downloads and /tmp for downloaded archives (DMG, ZIP, PKG) with quarantine-attribute removal (xattr calls) or execution shortly after download. Correlate with process execution from those paths and unusual code-signing attribute modifications.

suggestion.title: VM/Sandbox Fingerprint Checking Evasion
suggestion.rationale: Article states fingerprinting is used 'to hide malware lures'—indicating conditional delivery: payload only executes on real macOS systems, not sandboxes. Detection must identify conditional VM/environment checks.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect processes querying Parallels/VMware/VirtualBox markers (ioreg output, sysctl hw.* queries), Docker socket presence, or known sandbox PID/PPID patterns. Conditional branching (fork/exit) based on VM detection is high-risk indicator of evasion-aware payload.

suggestion.title: ChatGPT Account Compromise — Bulk Phishing Template Generation
suggestion.rationale: Title explicitly states ChatGPT was used 'across multiple fraud schemes.' This is the core execution mechanism. Pipeline missed entirely. No detection for suspicious API request patterns, high-volume message generation, or account anomalies.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on ChatGPT accounts (compromised or abused) generating large batches of structurally-identical or near-identical social-engineering content (payment urgency, credential requests) in short time windows. Flag logins from new IP ranges immediately preceding template generation runs. Correlate API token reuse across multiple phishing campaign waves.

suggestion.title: Inbound Phishing — AI-Generated Content with Financial/Payment Themes
suggestion.rationale: Scam network sends phishing at scale via ChatGPT-generated content ('multiple fraud schemes'). Pipeline missed initial-access layer entirely — no detection for bulk phishing delivery or AI-signature phishing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag emails with ChatGPT linguistic fingerprints (unusual consistency, verbose explanations, JSON-like structures) claiming account compromise, payment holds, or urgent wire requests sent in bulk waves. Monitor for shortened URL redirects to compromised domains. Correlate sender domain registration timing with Poipet campaign windows.

suggestion.title: Account Takeover Post-Compromise — Forwarding Rules and Mailbox Delegation
suggestion.rationale: Scam operations require persistence in compromised business email. Pipeline missed persistence phase. No mention of mailbox rules, forwarding, or delegation abuse typical of Poipet-style campaigns.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect mailbox forwarding rules to external domains created within 10 min of password reset or anomalous login. Alert on inbox rules hiding flagged/phishing emails or deleting CEO-domain communications. Monitor delegated mailbox access grants to newly-created service accounts.

suggestion.title: Credential Harvesting — Phishing Form Hosting and Form Submission Capture
suggestion.rationale: Fraud schemes require credential collection ('multiple fraud schemes'). Article title implies targeting of employees or customers. Pipeline missed reconnaissance and credential-access phases.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Flag compromised internal or external domains hosting login forms or credential-entry pages linked in phishing campaigns. Monitor for successful logins followed immediately by anomalous API calls (mail sync, calendar export, user enumeration). Detect brute-force login attempts using credential-pair sets leaked from Poipet disruption.

suggestion.title: Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring — Scam Funds Exfiltration
suggestion.rationale: Fraud networks collect victim payments via cryptocurrency. No IOCs extracted for blockchain addresses despite 'critical' severity and known scam-network context. Pipeline missed impact/exfiltration layer.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cross-reference known Poipet scam wallet addresses (from OpenAI/regulatory advisories) against wire transfers, gift card purchases, and cryptocurrency exchange deposits. Alert on structuring patterns (small, frequent transfers) or consolidation into high-mixer-usage wallets. Monitor employee-reported fraud fund destinations.

suggestion.title: Domain Registration and Certificate Issuance — Phishing Infrastructure Hosting
suggestion.rationale: Scam networks register lookalike domains for phishing hosting. Pipeline returned no domain IOCs despite 'network' terminology implying infrastructure. Missing initial-access reconnaissance.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor WHOIS and Certificate Transparency for domains typosquatting financial institutions (banks, payment processors, cryptocurrency exchanges) registered during the Poipet campaign timeline with privacy proxies. Alert on rapid bulk domain registration with similar structural patterns (e.g., variations on 'secure-verify-confirm'). Correlate DNS resolutions to known scam IP ranges.

suggestion.title: Malicious Agent Import Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly describes attack vector as 'malicious agent imports' causing 'host command execution'—this is the primary exploitation path and requires detection of imported agents from untrusted sources or unsigned packages.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for import/load events of agents from external or unauthenticated sources. Flag instances where agent instantiation is followed immediately by spawned child processes (shells, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, /bin/bash) that the agent process does not normally execute.

suggestion.title: Host Command Execution from Agent Context
suggestion.rationale: Article states flaws 'let attackers run host commands'—direct command execution through the agent runtime is the impact, requiring detection of shell spawning from Paperclip AI processes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on process creation where Paperclip AI or identified agent executable is the parent, and child process is cmd.exe, powershell.exe, /bin/sh, /bin/bash, or other shell interpreter without legitimate application logic justifying it.

suggestion.title: Suspicious Dynamic Agent Module Loading
suggestion.rationale: Exploitation pathway involves 'agent imports' which implies dynamic module/package loading. Detection should surface atypical import patterns, missing signature validation, or loading from non-standard repositories.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor package manager logs, import hooks, or file access patterns for Paperclip agent runtime loading dependencies from unexpected network locations, unsigned packages, or paths not in standard package directories.

suggestion.title: Agent Framework Code Injection via Dependency Confusion
suggestion.rationale: Malicious agent imports suggest a supply-chain or dependency confusion attack. Detection should catch attempts to shadow legitimate Paperclip packages or agents with malicious versions.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate agent import attempts against known good package signatures and repositories. Flag attempts to load agents that fail validation or come from typosquatted package names, internal-only registries accessed externally, or sources with unusual geolocation/ownership.

suggestion.title: Privilege Escalation via Agent Execution Context
suggestion.rationale: If agents run in elevated context (system/root), malicious imports could enable privilege escalation. Article's severity (CRIT) and 'host commands' phrasing suggests escalation is part of the threat model.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for process creation events where a Paperclip agent spawns a shell or command executor at higher privilege level than the agent process itself, or attempts to run commands with sudo/RunAs tokens.

suggestion.title: Device Code Phishing Exploitation Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly states 'adoption has exploded from zero criminal kits in the wild to 25+ distinct kits (and counting)' with named operators: EvilTokens (340+ organizations in first five weeks), Kali365 (FBI advisory), ARToken, DEBULL, Forg365. Clear indication of active, measurable technique proliferation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for device code authentication flows (device_code grant type) initiated from external or suspicious sources, particularly those preceded by password failures. Flag rapid iteration of device code requests to different user accounts from same source IP, and alert on successful device code completions followed by anomalous access patterns indicative of admin-controlled payload activation.

suggestion.title: Adversary-in-the-Middle Phishing Kit Detection
suggestion.rationale: Article names Tycoon 2FA and other 'established AiTM vendors' as active operators, lists AiTM phishing as primary attack type alongside device code. Techniques used in conjunction: 'attempting device code phishing first, then falling back to AiTM if it times out.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect inline proxy/MITM patterns: TLS certificate mismatches on legitimate Microsoft/Google domains, HTTP-to-HTTPS downgrades within redirect chains, session cookie harvesting in proxy logs, and out-of-band MFA challenges during login. Correlate with browser fingerprinting checks (referrer validation, User-Agent inspection) immediately preceding auth attempts.

suggestion.title: Bot Protection and Fingerprinting Evasion Signatures
suggestion.rationale: Article states '95% of in-browser attacks that Push Security detects use some form of bot protection, often layered with referrer checks and browser fingerprinting.' This is an observable defense-evasion signature preceding successful phishing.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify HTTP responses containing bot-protection challenges (Cloudflare, Akamai), referrer header validation, or fingerprinting scripts that serve differential content by User-Agent, IP geolocation, or TLS version. Alert on phishing domains with layered checks that permit human browsers but block automated scanners—a signature pattern of attacker infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Rapid Phishing Domain Registration Clustering
suggestion.rationale: Article quantifies: '89% of phishing domains are now active for fewer than two days, with just 6.5% surviving past 15 days.' This ultra-short lifespan is a signature of AI-generated, disposable infrastructure and represents a traceable behavioral pattern.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cluster newly registered or first-observed domains by registrar, SSL issuer, ASN, and hosting provider. Alert on 5+ domains from the same infrastructure provider all resolving to phishing-indicative content (login page clones, bot-protection headers) within 24 hours. Flag domains with TTLs <48 hours registered within 6 hours of first traffic observation.

suggestion.title: Abuse of Legitimate SaaS Platforms for Phishing Delivery
suggestion.rationale: Article lists abuse of Cloudflare Workers, Railway, Vercel, Microsoft Dynamics, SharePoint, Adobe, Google Firebase, Google Sites, Jotform, Linode, Azure, Atlassian, and notes phishing 'increasingly abuses legitimate services — AI chatbot sharing features, search ad placement, in-app messages and app-generated emails — to inherit the domain reputation.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for atypical outbound traffic from legitimate SaaS domains (Vercel, Railway, Firebase, Dynamics, SharePoint) containing phishing characteristics: embedded login forms, credential exfiltration payloads, bot-protection redirects, or external link chains. Flag emails and in-app messages originating from these trusted platforms with external redirects or shortened URLs pointing to disposable infrastructure.

suggestion.title: Dynamic Payload Switching in Attacker-Controlled Phishing Kits
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'kits dynamically switching between payloads depending on the environment and target's behavior. For example, attempting device code phishing first, then falling back to AiTM if it times out.' Kits 'controlled by attacker-operated admin panels that give full control over the payload and when it's delivered.'
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate multiple authentication failures or timeout events from single source IP with subsequent changes in MFA challenge type (device_code → OTP → AiTM). Alert on sessions that retry authentication with different mechanisms within 2-5 minute windows, or on rapid payload switching patterns (e.g., device code request → redirect to phishing page → credential form) indicating admin-controlled activation.

suggestion.title: Anomalous Device Code Authentication Request Pattern
suggestion.rationale: Device code phishing attacks exploit the OAuth Device Authorization Grant flow. Article references device code as attack vehicle; pipeline should detect when legitimate device code endpoints (e.g., microsoft.com/devicelogin) are accessed from unusual geolocations, VPNs, or TOR, then followed by successful authentication to cloud tenants.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate device code portal visits (via proxy or EDR telemetry) with subsequent successful OAuth device code grant completions. Flag when device code auth is followed immediately by API calls from the same compromised token to high-sensitivity resources (Mail, SharePoint, Teams).

suggestion.title: Phishing Email Delivery of Device Code Registration Links
suggestion.rationale: Device code phishing typically begins with spearphishing emails directing users to enter a code at microsoft.com/devicelogin or similar. Article frames this as 'phishing' attack; pipeline missed credential-phishing initial-access vector entirely.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect phishing emails containing URLs to device code authentication portals, especially when URLs are obfuscated, use URL shorteners, or employ homograph attacks on microsoft.com/google.com domains. Correlate email delivery with user enrollment in device code flow within 10 minutes.

suggestion.title: Cloud Lateral Movement via Compromised Device Code Token
suggestion.rationale: Once attacker obtains device code via phishing, they use the resulting token to pivot. Article's mention of 'reasons why' threat is growing suggests evolved post-compromise behavior; pipeline should map lateral movement within cloud environment after device code compromise.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: After device code authentication, detect sudden spike in API calls to multiple cloud services (Exchange Online, SharePoint, Teams, Dynamics 365) from the authenticated token, especially bulk enumeration of shared mailboxes, file listing, or user/group discovery.

suggestion.title: Device Code Flow Without Matching Client Application
suggestion.rationale: Legitimate device code flow is used by specific applications; attackers may request codes for applications not expected in the environment. Article's threat relevance hinges on attack evolution; this detection addresses a telltale misuse signature.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor EntraIdAuditLogs for DeviceCodeFlow events where the requesting ClientApplicationId does not match organization's approved device code consumers (printers, IoT, legacy clients). Flag requests for consumer-facing clients (Office.com, Azure PowerShell) from non-standard OAuth scopes.

suggestion.title: Geographic Impossibility: Device Code Request to Token Redemption
suggestion.rationale: User at desk in New York receives phishing, visits device code portal. Attacker in China redeems token from their IP/geo. Pipeline should detect geographic inconsistencies in OAuth device flow steps to expose attackers redeeming stolen codes.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Correlate device code portal access logs with subsequent device code grant events in sign-in logs. Flag when the IP/geolocation of the user entering the code differs materially (>500 miles, different continent, unexpected country) from the IP redeeming the resulting auth token.

suggestion.title: Vulnerability Scanner Detection: CVE-2026-63077 in Active Results
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly references CVE-2026-63077 and recommends 'Standard asset-exposure hunt' via the asset-exposure template. Pipeline should generate a use case to detect when vulnerability scanners report this CVE as present on TeamCity instances.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor vulnerability scanner exports (Qualys, Nessus, Rapid7) for CVE-2026-63077 present on TeamCity assets. Filter to public-facing instances (agent polling protocol accessible externally). Escalate all detections as critical due to CISA KEV active exploitation status and 2026-08-08 remediation deadline.

suggestion.title: TeamCity Agent Polling Protocol Exploitation Attempt
suggestion.rationale: Article describes exploitation via 'agent polling protocol' — an application-layer protocol specific to TeamCity. Pipeline should generate a use case to detect anomalous or malicious requests to this protocol endpoint attempting to exploit the deserialization vulnerability.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect malformed, unauthenticated, or suspicious deserialization payloads sent to TeamCity agent polling endpoint. Look for serialized Java object attempts, exception stack traces in application logs indicating deserialization failures, failed agent authentication attempts, or unusual request patterns to agent listener ports.

suggestion.title: TeamCity Patch Compliance: Version Inventory vs. Patched Baseline
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies federal patch due date (2026-08-08) and recommends asset-exposure hunting. Pipeline should generate a use case to validate TeamCity instances are running patched versions and alert on vulnerable instances post-deadline.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Cross-reference TeamCity instance inventory against known-vulnerable version ranges (pre-patch). Alert on any instances running unpatched versions on or after 2026-08-08 remediation deadline. Correlate with network topology to identify publicly exposed instances as highest priority.

suggestion.title: Post-Exploitation RCE: Anomalous Process Execution from TeamCity Agent
suggestion.rationale: Article describes RCE via deserialization; pipeline should generate a detection use case for post-exploitation activity (command execution) originating from compromised TeamCity build agents running arbitrary code outside normal build contexts.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor TeamCity agent processes (java.exe with agent libraries) for execution of unusual child processes, shell spawns, or reverse-shell indicators outside normal build-artifact production. Correlate with failed or suspicious build job invocations preceding anomalous process activity.

suggestion.title: Network Boundary: External Access to TeamCity Agent Polling Ports
suggestion.rationale: Article emphasizes exploitation via public-facing agent polling protocol. Pipeline should generate a network-layer detection use case for external access attempts to TeamCity agent listeners from untrusted sources.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Alert on inbound network traffic to TeamCity agent polling ports (default ~9090) originating from external or untrusted IP ranges. Assess whether traffic is consistent with expected agent registration patterns or represents potential exploitation attempts. Escalate if traffic contains serialized Java object payloads or fails agent-protocol authentication handshake.

suggestion.title: TeamCity Public Exposure & Unauthenticated Access
suggestion.rationale: Article states vulnerability 'could allow unauthenticated remote code execution via the agent polling protocol'—asset-exposure hunt for TeamCity services accessible without credentials is the canonical first detection step for CISA KEV entries.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Identify TeamCity build agent listening ports (default 9090, configurable) exposed to untrusted networks. Cross-reference with vulnerability scanner results for CVE-2026-63077 to find instances not yet patched despite federal due date 2026-08-08. Flag any inbound connection attempts to agent polling endpoints from external IP ranges.

suggestion.title: Java Deserialization Payload in TeamCity Agent Protocol
suggestion.rationale: Article explicitly identifies attack vector as 'deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability'—typical Java deserialization exploits (ysoserial gadget chains) are detectable in network traffic and logs.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor TeamCity agent polling protocol traffic for serialized Java objects (magic bytes `aced0005` in network dumps indicate Java serialization). Correlate with abnormal child process spawning under TeamCity build agent user context. Flag any `Runtime.exec()` or similar gadget chain indicators in protocol handshakes.

suggestion.title: CVE-2026-63077 Exploitation Attempts
suggestion.rationale: Article assigns CVE-2026-63077 as the primary tracking ID; detection rules should key off CVE ID for early correlation with known exploit signatures and public proof-of-concept code.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Ingest CVE-2026-63077 detections from Qualys, Tenable, or equivalent scanners. Correlate with network traffic anomalies to TeamCity agent ports within 24 hours of scan completion. Cross-check SOAR/WAF logs for payloads matching known public exploits (e.g., CVE-2026-63077 proof-of-concept repository commits).

suggestion.title: Abnormal Agent Polling Protocol Traffic
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies attack surface as 'agent polling protocol'—legitimate protocol abuse is harder to detect than outbound C2 but requires baseline of normal polling behavior for comparison.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Establish baseline for normal TeamCity agent polling frequency, payload size, and message types. Alert on deviations: sudden increases in polling rate, oversized payloads, or polling from unexpected internal subnets. Flag out-of-band polling attempts to non-standard TeamCity build agent ports.

suggestion.title: TeamCity RCE Post-Exploitation Process Activity
suggestion.rationale: Article outcome is 'unauthenticated remote code execution'—post-exploitation child processes spawned under TeamCity user context are high-fidelity indicators regardless of exploit variant.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Monitor for unexpected child processes spawned by TeamCity build agent or server processes (teamcity.exe, buildAgent.exe, or equivalent). Flag reverse shells, data exfiltration commands, or lateral movement tools (psexec, wmiexec). Correlate with network indicators to confirm exploitation vs. legitimate build job.

suggestion.title: TeamCity Internet Exposure (CVE-2026-63077)
suggestion.rationale: Article states 'unauthenticated remote code execution' and CISA KEV guarantees active exploitation; asset exposure is the canonical hunt. Article provides explicit template guidance ('Substitute this CVE wherever the template references `<CVE>`') but no use case was instantiated.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect inbound connections from external IPs to TeamCity agent polling port (10123) or management UI (8080/443). Correlate with software inventory to identify exposed systems running versions vulnerable to CVE-2026-63077. Flag any with patch date >2026-08-08.

suggestion.title: TeamCity Agent Polling Protocol Exploitation
suggestion.rationale: Article specifies vulnerability is in 'agent polling protocol' but no protocol-level detection was generated for this specific attack surface despite it being the exploitation vector.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect malformed or anomalous agent polling protocol frames: oversized payloads, embedded serialized Java objects, deserialization errors, or protocol negotiation failures. Legitimate agents should only connect from trusted internal infrastructure.

suggestion.title: TeamCity RCE Post-Exploitation Process Spawning
suggestion.rationale: Article describes 'remote code execution' but no post-exploitation detection was created despite this being essential for incident hunt and response workflows following successful exploitation.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Detect unexpected child processes (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, /bin/sh) spawned by java.exe or teamcityd processes shortly after anomalous network activity. Monitor for encoded payloads, network beaconing, or credential access behaviors initiated by TeamCity server processes.

suggestion.title: TeamCity Patch Compliance Inventory
suggestion.rationale: Article warns 'patch lag is the silent killer' and includes federal patch due date 2026-08-08; pipeline should generate inventory-based compliance hunts regardless of active exploitation signals.
suggestion.detection_hypothesis: Query software inventory for JetBrains TeamCity; identify versions affected by CVE-2026-63077 (typically <2024.3.2 or <2025.1.2); cross-reference with external network exposure; escalate non-compliant systems to patch queue with federal deadline context.

suggestion.title: TeamCity Unauthenticated Agent Polling Anomalies
